abstract: Microtubules are organized into functionally distinct subsets that differ in stability, post-translational modifications (PTMs) and lattice spacing, but what defines these subsets and governs selective binding of motors and microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs) to specific subsets has remained unclear. Here, we demonstrate that the preferential motility of the motor protein Kinesin-1 along stable, long-lived microtubules depends on microtubule lattice spacing and MAP7 family members. Using Kinesin-1 truncations and MAP7 family depletions, we show that Kinesin-1 subset selectivity is not specified by its motor domain, but instead requires its coiled-coil 1 region, which mediates MAP7 binding. While depletion of all MAP7 proteins abolishes Kinesin-1 motility, loss of MAP7D1 alone results in non-selective motility, identifying MAP7D1 as the key determinant of selectivity. Using knock-out cells lacking detyrosinated and acetylated microtubules, we find that MAP7D1 enrichment on stable microtubule subsets depends on lattice structure rather than PTMs, whereas in vitro reconstitution assays directly demonstrate that MAP7D1 preferentially binds expanded microtubule lattices characteristic of long-lived microtubules. Together, our results establish microtubule lattice conformation as a key determinant of cellular microtubule subset identity and selective binding of MAPs.
